newsitem.title: QATAR: FEATURE-Qatar prepares for "crucial" Gulf Arab summit.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Qatar prepares for "crucial" Gulf Arab summit.

text.p: Qatar has started preparing for a showpiece Gulf Arab summit expected to prove a watershed in the history of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), Qatari officials and diplomats said.
Diplomats say strains are growing in the 16-year-old alliance as festering border rows and political differences take a toll.

"It's going to be a very crucial summit...its outcome may make or break the future of the GCC", said a senior Qatar foreign affairs ministry official. "But we, as a host, would not do anything to hamper its unity".
The rulers of the GCC, grouping Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), hold a summit every year in December in member countries by rotation.
This year it is to be held in Qatar, and diplomats expect it to take place on December 22-24 although no date has been set.
"There are more than a dozen outstanding border issues among GCC members begging resolution for decades", said a Western diplomat.

"Many of them directly concern the leader Saudi Arabia itself, which has border problems with Qatar, Kuwait and Oman. Some have even led to near-armed conflicts, like the one between Qatar and Bahrain in 1986 and Saudi Arabia and Qatar in 1991. But none of them has been resolved", he said.
"On the economic front also the GCC's balance-sheet has drawn blank", said an Arab diplomat.

"In 1981, the organisation was formed with an avowed goal of creating a well-knit, formidable economic, political and military bloc with a single common market and currency. But 16 years on, it has not been able to agree on even a common customs tariff".

The Arab diplomat said: "GCC leadership does not accept controversial issues and dissent and will try to avoid the contentious topics, such as border disputes and political differences. But how far it succeeds in avoiding the issues will depend on members' cooperation concerned with the issue".

Last year, Qatar's delegation walked out in protest from the closing session of the Muscat summit over a procedural wrangle in the appointment of the current secretary general, Jameel al-Hujilan of Saudi Arabia, when its dissent was ignored.
This year, Bahrain threatened to boycott the Doha summit if Qatar did not withdraw a case it filed with the International Court of Justice over a territorial row with Manama.
Qatar has said it would only withdraw the case if Saudi mediation to solve the dispute succeeded.

"However, Qataris have not taken Bahrain's threat as serious", said a Western diplomat. "But they do fear that an immediate neighbour's unhelpful attitude might hinder the objective they hope to achieve from the summit they are hosting for the third time".
Doha hosted the GCC summit in 1990, when Gulf states resolved to put their armies under the command of the U.S.-led international coalition which liberated Kuwait from Iraqi occupation.
It also hosted the GCC summit in 1982, when a unified economic accord known as the Doha Declaration was adopted.

This time, the Qataris intend to use the occasion as a public relations and media blitz to project an image of a resurgent nation with progressive policies and strategic economic and political importance.
"They have long been portrayed as a backwater in the backyard of the regional power, Saudi Arabia, and have been trying to emerge from the shadow of the Kingdom", the Western diplomat said.
"The coming summit will naturally give them a chance and the chairmanship of the GCC for the next months to assert their maverick policies which have made their more conservative neighbours sit up".
Qatar, whose present ruler, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani, deposed his father in June 1995, has promised grassroots democracy by holding municipal elections.

It has also befriended radical Shi'ite Iran, restored ties with Gulf war foe Iraq and moved faster than any other Gulf state in establishing economic ties with Israel -- initiatives all largely at odds with Saudi policies.

In preparing for the summit, Qatari authorities have hired around half a dozen firms to refurbish all roads and corniches leading to the conference centre and give the city of 260,000 a festive look by the end of November.
